newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel-PLO war of words escalates.
newsitem.headline: Israel-PLO war of words escalates.

text.p: Israel and the PLO have stepped up a war of words, ignoring U.S. calls to revive a spirit of partnership in peace ahead of an American mediation mission.
U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross returns to the region this weekend in an attempt to calm tensions after two Islamic suicide bombers killed 13 people in a Jerusalem market on July 30.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu kept pressure on Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Thursday to crack down on Moslem militants.

"He can crush Hamas militarily. It's not that he can't, but that he doesn't want to," Netanyahu told members of his Likud party. "He continues to preserve their ability (to attack Israel)... in order to pressure Israel and achieve his goals."
Arafat lashed out at Netanyahu in an Israeli newspaper interview, saying the prime minister "has declared war on us and we have to prepare for what will come".
A State Department spokesman called Arafat's statement counterproductive "to the extent that (it) is... interpreted as meaning battle with Israel".

After the market attack, Israel halted peace talks with the PLO and sealed off the West Bank and Gaza, stopping trade and keeping thousands of Palestinians from jobs in Israel. Israel's Treasury froze transfer of tax duties it owes the Palestinians.

Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi, in Israel for a memorial service for four Italian peacekeepers killed in the crash of a U.N. helicopter in south Lebanon, said he asked Netanyahu on Thursday for a goodwill act towards Palestinians.

"Netanyahu told me that he is ready to take goodwill measures as long as there is a corresponding act of specific action against terrorism by Arafat," Prodi said at a news conference in Tel Aviv following talks with the Israeli leader.
Netanyahu insisted in a speech at Likud headquarters that he would not allow the Israeli blockade to lead to a food shortage in Palestinian self-rule areas.
An Israeli military official said the army would allow 20 truckloads of food, medicine, animal feed and other essentials into Gaza on Friday.

State Department spokesman Barry Rubin criticised Israeli and Palestinian leaders for attacking each other publicly after Secretary of State Madeleine Albright urged both sides to renew a spirit of partnership in peace.
Rubin said during a daily briefing that Arafat and his Palestinian Authority "should refrain from... statements that cast doubt on the peace that they have committed themselves to."

He was also asked about remarks Netanyahu made during a news conference with Jordan's Crown Prince Hassan on Wednesday in which he accused the Palestinian Authority of behaving "like a regime facilitating terror, like Iran, or Iraq or Libya".
Rubin said it was hard to understand how Arafat could be compared to Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi.

"Chairman Arafat was on the White House lawn with the president. He signed a peace agreement with the Israelis. We regard him as a partner in our effort to find peace in the Middle East. Colonel Gaddafi is an international outlaw."
All sides welcomed Albright's saying she might at month's end visit the region.

"There was a call between her and me yesterday and I thanked her for her speech which she made yesterday that showed the care of the U.S. to push the peace process and save it from the current crisis," Arafat told reporters in Gaza.
"We will welcome her and anyone else who can help restore security," Netanyahu said.
Israel and the PLO were on the brink of renewing committee-level talks on confidence-building measures, such as opening air and sea ports in Gaza when the suicide bombers struck.
Formal peace negotiations were suspended in March after Israel broke ground for a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
